title: Should I generate missing B-roll or film a pickup for a customer story?
summary: Choose supporting visuals for a customer story based on what they need to show: the real product, general context, or an explicitly illustrative idea.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Decide what the missing picture must establish before choosing its source.
- Search existing authorized footage before inventing a replacement.
- Keep illustrative imagery distinguishable from documentary customer evidence.


## Ask why the edit needs another picture


The missing shot may need to explain a product action, establish a workplace, or cover a join between interview excerpts. Those purposes call for different solutions. A pickup showing a real interface can answer the first; a restrained graphic might answer the second; staying on the speaker may solve the third.


In an illustrative case study, a customer explains assigning a reviewer to a cut. If the viewer needs to see how that happens, capture the real product interaction. A generated image of someone at a laptop does not demonstrate the assignment workflow, even if it looks convincing.


## Search the material you already own


Check the shoot's supporting folders, prior approved product captures, and appropriate customer footage. You may already have a useful process shot that was not labeled for this story. Confirm that its product version and intended use fit the current edit.


In Wideframe, identify the relevant folders and use the[visual-search recipe](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/find-clips-visual/) to look for the concrete action. Ask for a few candidates rather than any image that matches the mood. A missing match is useful information; it tells you what still needs to be obtained.


## Choose a pickup for a specific real-world claim


A pickup is valuable when the shot must show a real person, place, physical product, or current interface. Keep the request small and purposeful: the exact action, framing, beginning and end, and any detail the audience must read. A targeted capture can be more useful than another broad day of footage.


Plan the shot around the sentence it supports. If the customer discusses a handoff, show enough of the handoff to understand it. Do not collect a beautiful close-up that leaves the essential action off screen. The edit's need should define the pickup.


## Use stock for general context with care


Stock can provide a broad location, atmosphere, or conceptual transition when it is suitable and licensed for the intended use. Avoid presenting an unrelated office or group of people as the actual customer's operation. The image's placement and any labels affect what the viewer will infer.


Choose footage that does not introduce extra claims. An industrial shot may imply a manufacturing process; a medical setting may imply a use case. If the customer story does not establish those associations, a simpler image or graphic may be clearer.


## Use generation for illustration, not replacement testimony


Generative tools can create imagery that did not come from the customer shoot. Descript's[current product page](https://www.descript.com/video-editing) , for example, includes generated visuals within its editing offering. That capability does not make the result documentary evidence of the customer's experience.


An abstract visualization of a tangled process can be appropriate when clearly illustrative. A fabricated customer workplace, person, or product interaction can imply facts that never happened. Do not use generated speech or imagery to create a customer endorsement. Keep the real interview at the center of the case study.


## Sometimes the best replacement is no replacement


A strong answer can remain on the customer's face. A clean visible cut may be less distracting than an irrelevant insert. A short title can explain the subject without manufacturing an event. Consider these options before adding media just to keep the frame moving.


If you need to hide a join, first ensure the audio edit preserves meaning. Covering the picture does not fix a misleading splice. Choose a visual that serves the sentence, and let a meaningful pause remain when the customer's delivery benefits from it.


## Finish with a consistent visual contract


Review the whole sequence and ask what each source appears to represent. Real customer footage, current product captures, stock context, and illustration can coexist when their roles are clear. Use labels where needed and avoid graphics that make an illustrative sequence look like recorded proof.


Keep the chosen assets and their source information with the project. For the next shoot, use the missing pictures to create a concise pickup list in advance. Wideframe can help find usable material; a well-defined visual need tells you when finding is enough and when filming is the better choice.


## Try this request


TRY AN EXAMPLE REQUEST


Find existing footage that clearly shows \[specific action\] for this customer statement. Use only the listed source folders and distinguish exact matches from general context. If the action is missing, describe the pickup we need rather than substituting unrelated imagery.
